rec7Vm5QNrDbc9sdb.Bio: Chance Garton is the host and producer of the Innerverse Podcast, where for over a decade he has investigated consciousness, mythology, symbolism, terrain health, and the psychosomatic language of the human body and mind. A biofield tuning practitioner, he uses tuning forks to help clients resolve physical symptoms, break negative patterns, and return to energetic coherence.

recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Bio: Kyle Denton is a community herbalist and medicine maker from Wisconsin who founded Tippecanoe Herbs with his wife Serena Marinelli in 2015. From their Milwaukee apothecary they craft small batch remedies from locally harvested and organic herbs, working from a bio terrain philosophy that blends Ayurveda with Western herbalism. He also runs Root Radical Herbal Academy, has taught for over a decade through his annual three season class and his Milwaukee herb walks, and sees clients as the Tuning Herbalist, using tuning forks to read the biofield. His Substack and podcast, Resonature, explore the interval between vital herbalism, biofield tuning and cosmology.
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Name: Kyle Denton
recbqsYSV8FGvCA28.Role: Community herbalist, founder of Tippecanoe Herbs

fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "The alternative is the native", "body": "Chance Garton opens by taking apart the word alternative. What the culture calls alternative medicine, he argues, is actually the native thing, while the allopathic system is the alter native, taking what nature gave, inverting it, and handing it back as poison called medicine. He also refuses the phrase side effects, saying side effects are simply effects. That framing sets up the whole conversation with Kyle Denton of Tippecanoe Herbs, whose Milwaukee shop forages its own plants, works with local farmers, and makes every medicine it sells in an apothecary kitchen behind the counter."}, {"title": "Foundations instead of memorized uses", "body": "Kyle Denton describes spinning his wheels early on, memorizing that peppermint is for an upset stomach. His breakthrough was learning foundational energetic patterns rather than plant to ailment pairs. He came up through an Ayurvedic training, translating Vata, Pitta and Kapha back into air, fire, earth, water and ether, then overlapped that grid onto Western herbalism, Greek medicine and the four humors, Appalachian folk medicine and Native American practice. Now he asks a person whether their complaint feels hot or cold, tense or loose, dry or damp, and matches it to a plant that heats, cools, dries or moistens."}, {"title": "The map is not the terrain", "body": "The conversation keeps circling a single idea, that language is a map and the felt quality is the terrain. Chance Garton argues that an inverted culture puts the name before the feeling, so people cannot know a plant without a label and an authority to supply it. Kyle Denton agrees but adds a yes and, since categorizing is a real human gift and the scaffolding of names is useful once the feeling comes first. His teaching aim follows from this. He does not hand students authority, he reminds them they already carry it."}, {"title": "Kronos, Kairos and the wobble in the year", "body": "Chance Garton floats a suspicion that time does not run in perfect cycles, that a year may not be exactly 365.25 days and that nature carries wiggle. He borrows the Greek pair Kronos, measured clock time shown by the sky clock, and Kairos, subjective felt time. Kyle Denton says he sees it in a decade of annual herb walks, including an Earth Day walk cancelled by a foot of snow, and pictures the calendar as an oval rather than a circle. Enslavement, they conclude, only happens when Kronos is placed ahead of Kairos."}, {"title": "Reading the young lung tincture", "body": "Kyle Denton walks through the young lung tincture he sent Chance Garton, and through the doctrine of signatures, which he credits to Paracelsus around 1511. Elecampane, read as Helen of the Campania, he says dispels green and yellow mucus and suits those who feel foreign or unable to speak. Rosemary and osha are fellow aromatics, each with a different major. New England Aster, yellow centered with purple rays that open and close, he uses to relax the diaphragm. In his account plantain heals mucosal tissue and Solomon's seal acts as a gentle activator. Nature, he says, reuses patterns the way Rupert Sheldrake described morphic fields."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Kyle Denton is the head hippie in charge of potion preparation at his family company, Tippecanoe Herbs. Join us to discover the doctrine of signatures in the patterns of plants, to know through consciousness the virtues of vegetation without the need to memorize Latin names and categories.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension we talk about Kyle's philosophy for herbal blends and different dosages, astro-aromatics and the scents of Aries, using the spirit of the plant for medicine without needing the physical, and many more vital ideas.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Matching the medicine to the person in front of you", "body": "Kyle Denton describes his formulation philosophy as starting from the individual rather than the herb. He separates material doses, meant to resolve a physical complaint, from smaller spiritual doses aimed at emotional patterns, and he chooses between tea, tincture or salve based on what a client will actually use. He credits his teacher Matthew Wood for the idea of nudgeopathy, the view that some constitutions respond to force while others open only to gentle influence. Chance Garton compares this to bodywork and sound, where a subtle signal can sometimes accomplish what a forceful adjustment cannot."}, {"title": "Consciousness first, expression second", "body": "Chance Garton brings in Neville Goddard's book Your Faith Is Your Fortune, reading it as a teaching that people become conscious of something before it expresses in their lives, not the reverse. He frames the healer as a conduit who holds awareness of wholeness and then witnesses it unfold. Kyle Denton relates this to moments when a plant brings a particular person to mind, and to reading signals from the stars, the seasons and plant signatures. Both treat this ordering of consciousness, language and outcome as a thread running through the whole conversation."}, {"title": "Astro Aromatics and the craft of incense", "body": "Kyle Denton explains his Astro Aromatics class, where he builds incense for each zodiac sign from the feeling a plant gives rather than from correspondence tables. Using Aries as the example, he describes dragon's blood as carrying a sharp, competitive edge and clove as a hot burning helper, rolled into spear shapes that Chance Garton notes burn hottest at the start. Kyle says he rolls incense with a clear mind because he thinks of each stick as a small prayer. Chance adds a playful wordplay reading of aromatics, tying it to love and to Attis, a spring regeneration figure."}, {"title": "Scent, memory and the dulled modern senses", "body": "Chance Garton suggests that modern people have lost sensitivity to smell and sound because of artificial fragrances, cleaners and constant background noise, recalling the silence of waking in a tent at a festival. He asks whether a weak sense of smell can be trained. Kyle Denton says it can, and describes students in his classes suddenly recalling vivid childhood scenes from a single scent. He frames aromatics as a shift in consciousness that relocates a person into memory. Chance proposes using a scent as an anchor, so that a practiced inner state can be revisited later through smell."}, {"title": "Imagination, plant spirits and the healing response", "body": "Kyle Denton describes imagining peppermint until he feels its cooling effect, and wonders aloud whether a strong relationship with a plant lets him receive its pattern without taking it. Chance Garton calls imagination a sensory apparatus and shares a shamanic journey that he says taught him to project the feeling of selenite. The two then discuss symptoms, with Kyle calling himself a vitalist who sees some illnesses as upgrades and stresses building vitality before any purge. Chance cautions about vibration near the teeth and suggests that resistance to symptoms, rather than the symptoms themselves, may be what causes harm."}]
